slides.text: Ireland is one of the least forested countries in Europe.

slides.caption: Just over 10% of Ireland's land is forest. The EU average is 39.8%, nearly four times higher.

slides.text: Forests aren't just scenery. Under Ireland's climate law, they're one of the tools meant to help pull the country to net zero.
slides.footer: Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act commits to a 51% emissions cut by 2030 and net-zero by 2050.

slides.text: Growing Ireland's forest cover is a core piece of the Climate Action Plan, alongside restoring wetlands and peat bogs. It relies on two things together: better management of the forest already in the ground, and afforestation, planting entirely new ground.
slides.footer: The plan targets about 8,000 hectares of new planting a year, alongside rehabilitating roughly 77,600 hectares of peatland by 2030.

slides.text: Every hectare of healthy forest is doing quiet, constant work pulling carbon out of the air.
slides.footer: Ireland's forests already hold an estimated 312 million tonnes of carbon.

slides.text: Right now, Ireland's forests are a net carbon sink. That's about to change. A large share of that forest is reaching maturity and being cut for commercial timber.
slides.footer: It's also a chance to replant with a more diverse mix of trees that better support wildlife, which is exactly why continued afforestation matters.

slides.text: This isn't a new problem. It's the tail end of a very old one.
slides.footer: Ireland was once far more heavily forested.

slides.text: Centuries of clearance for farmland, fuel and timber stripped Ireland's woodland cover to almost nothing.
slides.footer: Much of it happened under British rule. By the early 20th century, forest cover had fallen to around 1%.

slides.caption: From a low point of roughly 1% at the start of the 1900s, forest cover has climbed back to about 10% today, still far short of where it started, and far short of the EU average.

slides.text: Unfortunately, most of the recovery hasn't been oak or ash. It's been Sitka spruce, a fast-growing conifer planted in rows.
slides.footer: Non-native, originally from the Pacific Northwest, it now dominates Ireland's commercial forestry.

slides.text: Grown in tight, single-species blocks, these plantations are widely called ecological dead zones.
slides.footer: Clear-felled every 40-50 years. They crowd out native plants, support little wildlife, and can acidify nearby soil and waterways.

slides.text: It's happening across Ireland's commercial forests right now.
slides.footer: Clear-felling removes an entire plantation block in one pass, not just mature trees.

slides.text: There's a growing recognition that Ireland needs more than commercial conifer. Native, mixed-species forest supports far more biodiversity, and diversifying away from pure Sitka is now part of the conversation.
slides.footer: But not everyone got that message.

slides.title: In 2026, a children's book sent to Irish primary schools told a very different message.

slides.text: Farmers are caught in the middle. Forestry means decades of tied-up land for a payoff that only arrives at harvest, competing directly with agriculture for the same fields.
slides.footer: Grant schemes have long made Sitka the fastest-paying option to plant, which is part of why it became the default.

slides.caption: The appetite is there. A 2022 survey of 1,000 adults found three in four people in Ireland want to see more forests, not fewer.
slides.footer: The question isn't whether people want more forest. It's what kind.

slides.text: Ireland's newer schemes are trying to shift the mix: a 2023 Forestry Programme built around climate-smart forestry, and a €45 million grant scheme for more sustainable, mixed-species management.
slides.footer: The direction is right. The scale, so far, isn't matching the 8,000 hectare-a-year target.

slides.text: Not every hectare has to look like a Sitka block. Native woodland can still take root, even now.
slides.footer: Mixed, native planting supports far more life than a single-species plantation ever will.

slides.text: Getting from 10% to anywhere near the European average means two things happening at once: planting a lot more, and planting differently.
slides.bold: a lot more, and planting differently
slides.footer: Native broadleaf mixed in with commercial conifer. Incentives that pay farmers for more than fast timber. A plan that treats forests as long-term infrastructure, not a line item.
